query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding oxygen as an interstitial dopant to a HfZrTi-based HEA promotes the formation of ordered oxygen complexes, which in turn enhances ductility and toughness by facilitating extra strain hardening and delaying dislocation motion.
generation.material_initial_state: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy prepared via conventional arc-melting, exhibiting a baseline yield strength of ~810 MPa and elongation of ~10.8%.
generation.intervention: Controlled oxygen doping (e.g., using TiO2) to form an O-doped HEA (often denoted as the O-2 HEA).
generation.conditions: Arc-melting in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere with oxygen content adjusted to yield approximately 2 at.% interstitial oxygen, leading to the formation of ordered oxygen complexes.
generation.mechanism: The interstitial oxygen atoms form ordered complexes within the severely distorted bcc lattice. These complexes impede dislocation motion and enhance strain hardening, which improves ductility (e.g., increased elongation) and toughness, while also moderately increasing yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxygen-doped HEA is anticipated to exhibit a yield strength of around 1138 MPa and an elongation of ~20%, representing a substantial improvement in ductility and toughness compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated HfZrTi-based HEA (specifically Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi) with ~810 MPa yield strength and ~10.8% elongation.
generation.boundary: The ductility and toughness enhancement depend on achieving the right oxygen content and proper processing to form about 18.5% ordered oxygen complexes; too much or too little oxygen or deviations in processing might not produce the desired effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact oxygen concentration and processing parameters required for optimal improvement in ductility and toughness still need to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate several batches of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEAs with controlled oxygen levels, including a baseline (no added oxygen), low oxygen, and target oxygen content. Process all samples using identical arc-melting and drop-casting conditions, then perform tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Microstructural characterization using TEM/EDS to confirm the presence and distribution of ordered oxygen complexes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped samples do not show a statistically significant increase in ductility (e.g., from ~10.8% to ~20% elongation) and fail to exhibit the formation of ordered oxygen complexes compared to the baseline sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
